    "enable.auto.commit": "false",    # manual commit for at-least-once
})
consumer.subscribe(["orders"])
while True:
    msg = consumer.poll(timeout=1.0)
    if msg and not msg.error():
        process(json.loads(msg.value()))
        consumer.commit()  # commit only after successful processing

words.etymology: Named after the novelist Franz Kafka by its original developer Jay Kreps, who chose it partly because Kafka was 'a system optimized for writing' — an apt metaphor for an append-only log. The name was intended to sound technical and is now inseparably associated with the distributed streaming platform.

words.shortDefinition: Multiple worker instances competing to claim and process messages from a single queue — each message processed once.
words.simpleDefinition: The competing consumer pattern deploys multiple worker instances that all consume from the same queue or Kafka consumer group. Each message is claimed and processed by exactly one worker — the broker ensures no two workers receive the same message. This provides horizontal scalability (add more workers to increase throughput) and fault tolerance (if one worker fails, others continue processing). It is the natural pattern for work queue processing, command handling, and any workload where tasks are independent and order within the queue does not matter.
words.longDefinition: The competing consumer pattern (described by Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf in 'Enterprise Integration Patterns') solves the throughput ceiling of single-threaded message processing. A single consumer can only process messages as fast as it can handle each one. By deploying N competing consumers on the same queue, throughput scales roughly linearly with N. In RabbitMQ and SQS, each message is exclusively claimed by one consumer — once a consumer receives a message and acknowledges it, other consumers cannot see it. In Kafka, the competing consumer pattern is implemented via consumer groups: each consumer group member is assigned an exclusive partition, so within a group, each message (on a given partition) is delivered to exactly one group member. Adding consumer instances increases the group's aggregate throughput up to the number of partitions. Competing consumers require tasks to be independent — if processing message B depends on the result of message A, and A and B go to different consumers, coordination becomes complex. In such cases, partition-by-key routing (routing all messages for the same entity to the same consumer) preserves ordering within an entity while maintaining inter-entity parallelism. Competing consumers are also the natural model for saga command processing: a saga orchestrator publishes a command to a topic, and the target service's consumer group processes it on whichever instance claims the message.
words.connector: Think of the competing consumer pattern like a dispatch center with multiple taxi drivers waiting for the next job — when a ride request comes in, the first available driver claims it. Other drivers do not also drive to the same address; only one goes.
words.techContext: We scale our order processing workers horizontally using the competing consumer pattern — at peak traffic we run 24 Kafka consumer instances across 24 partitions, each independently processing order commands without any coordination overhead.
words.exampleSentence: The competing consumer pattern allowed us to scale shipment processing from 500 to 8,000 tasks per minute by simply adding worker instances — no code changes, just more consumers on the same Kafka consumer group.

codeExample.code:
# Kubernetes: scale competing consumers horizontally
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-processor
spec:
  replicas: 12   # 12 competing consumers on the orders topic
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-processor
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: order-processor:v2.1.0
          env:
            - name: KAFKA_GROUP_ID
              value: order-processing-group  # same group = competing
            - name: KAFKA_TOPIC
              value: orders

words.etymology: Competing from Latin competere ('to strive together') — multiple parties seeking the same resource. Consumer from Latin consumere ('to take up, to use'). Pattern from the 'Enterprise Integration Patterns' catalog (Hohpe and Woolf, 2003), where it is listed as the Competing Consumers pattern.

words.shortDefinition: Publishing one event to a topic so multiple independent subscribers each receive their own copy.
words.simpleDefinition: Fanout is the messaging pattern where a single published event is delivered to multiple independent consumers or consumer groups, each receiving their own copy to process independently. Unlike the competing consumer pattern (where consumers share messages from a queue), fanout delivers the same message to every subscriber. In Kafka, fanout is the natural behavior of multiple consumer groups on the same topic — each group maintains its own offset and receives all events independently. In RabbitMQ, fanout exchanges route each message to all bound queues simultaneously.
words.longDefinition: Fanout is fundamental to event-driven microservices architectures. When an Order service publishes an OrderCreated event, multiple downstream services need to act: Inventory must reserve stock, Billing must create an invoice, Notifications must email the customer, and Analytics must record the event for reporting. These are independent concerns served by independent services. Fanout delivers the same event to all of them without the Order service knowing or caring how many consumers exist. In Kafka, this is the default behavior: each consumer group is independently positioned in the topic, and adding a new consumer group for a new service requires zero changes to the producer. This is a significant architectural advantage over point-to-point queues, where the producer must explicitly route to each consumer. Fanout enables the open/closed principle at the messaging layer: the Order service is closed for modification (no code changes needed) but open for extension (new services subscribe without touching the publisher). The trade-off is that fanout creates implicit dependencies — removing an event or changing its schema breaks all subscribers silently. Schema registries (Confluent Schema Registry with Avro) and consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) enforce compatibility at the fanout boundary.
words.connector: Think of fanout like a television broadcast — one station transmits a signal and every TV in range receives it independently. The station does not know or care how many TVs are tuned in, and adding a new TV does not require the station to do anything.
words.techContext: Our OrderCreated event fans out to six independent consumer groups — Inventory, Billing, Notifications, Analytics, Search, and Fraud — each processing the event independently at their own pace without any coupling to each other or to the Order service.
words.exampleSentence: Fanout architecture let us add a new real-time fraud scoring consumer to the order events topic without touching a single line of the Order service code.

codeExample.code:
# Producer: publish once to a topic
producer.produce(
    topic="order-events",
    key=order_id.encode(),
    value=json.dumps({"type": "OrderCreated", "orderId": order_id, ...}).encode()
)
# ONE publish → fanout to ALL consumer groups

# Consumer group 1: Inventory Service
consumer_inventory = Consumer({"group.id": "inventory-svc", ...})
consumer_inventory.subscribe(["order-events"])  # gets ALL events

# Consumer group 2: Billing Service (independent offset)
consumer_billing = Consumer({"group.id": "billing-svc", ...})
consumer_billing.subscribe(["order-events"])    # gets ALL events independently

# Adding a new consumer group requires ZERO changes to the producer

words.etymology: Fan from Dutch vaan ('banner') — something that spreads out from a central point. Fanout from electronics engineering, where fanout describes the number of logic gate inputs that can be driven by a single gate output. In messaging, adopted as a metaphor for one-to-many delivery.

words.shortDefinition: Propagating trace context across service calls so a single request's path through the system can be visualized.
words.simpleDefinition: Distributed tracing tracks a single user request as it crosses service boundaries, threading together the spans from each service into a complete end-to-end timeline. Each service creates a span that records its work, annotated with the trace ID and parent span ID received from the caller. A tracing backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog APM) collects all spans and reconstructs the full request path, showing which services were called, in what order, how long each took, and where errors occurred. Without it, diagnosing latency or failures in a multi-service call chain requires correlating logs across dozens of services manually.
words.longDefinition: In a monolith, a single stack trace shows the full request path. In a microservices system, a single user action may traverse 10–20 services — each running in its own process, on its own server, writing to its own log. Without distributed tracing, there is no way to reconstruct which downstream call was slow, which service introduced an error, or what the total end-to-end latency was for a given user request. Distributed tracing solves this by propagating context — a trace ID and parent span ID — through every service call. When Service A calls Service B over HTTP, it injects the traceparent header (W3C Trace Context standard) containing the trace ID and its own span ID. B extracts this context, creates a child span with A's span ID as parent, does its work, and calls C — injecting the updated context. A central trace collector (Jaeger, Zipkin) receives all spans and reconstructs the directed acyclic graph of the request. At async boundaries (Kafka messages), trace context must be explicitly injected into message headers and extracted on consumption, as described in the transactional messaging chapter. The OpenTelemetry SDK provides vendor-neutral instrumentation for HTTP, gRPC, and Kafka clients in all major languages. In the Microservices Patterns book, distributed tracing is presented as part of the observability trio alongside structured logging and metrics — the three pillars needed to make a distributed system understandable in production.
words.connector: Think of distributed tracing like a passport stamp at each border crossing — each country (service) stamps the same passport (trace ID) with the time you arrived and left. When something goes wrong, you can review the full itinerary and see exactly where the delay or problem occurred.
words.techContext: After adding OpenTelemetry distributed tracing across all 18 of our services, we diagnosed a 400ms p99 latency regression in 10 minutes — the flame graph showed the database query in the catalog service had acquired a table lock from a concurrent migration.
words.exampleSentence: Distributed tracing revealed that 85% of our checkout endpoint's latency was spent waiting for the fraud scoring service, which had been undetected in our per-service metrics because its own p50 looked healthy.

codeExample.code:
# OpenTelemetry: automatic HTTP instrumentation propagates trace context
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.requests import RequestsInstrumentor
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.flask import FlaskInstrumentor

# Auto-instrument: injects/extracts traceparent header on all HTTP calls
FlaskInstrumentor().instrument()
RequestsInstrumentor().instrument()

# Manual span for business logic
tracer = trace.get_tracer("order-service")

@app.post("/orders")
def create_order():
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("validate-order") as span:
        span.set_attribute("order.customer_id", request.json["customerId"])
        validate(request.json)
    # HTTP call to payment service automatically carries traceparent header
    payment = requests.post(
        "http://payment-service/reserves",
        json={"amount": request.json["total"]}
    )

words.etymology: Distributed from Latin distribuere ('to divide among'); tracing from Old French tracier ('to mark a path'). Distributed tracing as a concept was formalized in the Dapper paper (Sigelman et al., Google, 2010) and later popularized by the Zipkin and Jaeger open-source projects. The W3C Trace Context specification (2021) standardized the traceparent header format.
